summary: Describes practices for letting an authoritative name server operator provide one named server at multiple locations through shared unicast (anycast) addresses, improving distribution and reducing query latency. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Several copies of the same helper stand in different cities all answering to the same name, so you ask the closest one.

subtitle: Distributing DNS servers across the network using shared unicast addresses for better performance.

tldr.problem: DNS servers are often concentrated in a few locations, causing high latency for queries from distant parts of the network.
tldr.mechanism: Multiple copies of the same authoritative DNS server are run at different geographic and topologic locations, all using the same shared unicast address. Routing ensures clients connect to the nearest copy.
tldr.outcome: Queries reach a nearby server faster. The trade-off is operational complexity and the need to keep servers synchronized.

today: RFC 3258 remains an informational standard describing proven operational practices for distributing authoritative DNS servers. The techniques it describes are widely deployed by DNS operators and internet root nameserver operators to reduce query latency globally.

sections.title: Distributing Authoritative Name Servers
sections.content:
RFC 3258 describes a practical way to place authoritative DNS servers in multiple geographic and network locations without requiring dedicated address space or complex routing infrastructure. The goal is to reduce latency for DNS queries in areas where servers are scarce and to improve overall DNS availability.

Instead of using a full anycast infrastructure (as described in RFC 1546), this approach uses shared unicast addresses: multiple server instances share a single IP address and are distributed across the network. Each server instance listens on this shared address and also on a unique administrative address for management and zone file updates.
sections.eli5: DNS servers are spread to different places but answer to the same address. Your query goes to the closest one automatically.

sections.title: Server Setup and Network Architecture
sections.content:
Each participating server needs two network interfaces or addresses. The shared-unicast interface uses the common IP address and serves DNS queries only for zones the server is authoritative for. The administrative interface has a unique IP address and handles zone file distribution, zone transfers, and operational monitoring.

The organization operating the mesh must have an autonomous system number and use BGP to announce a route to the network containing the shared-unicast address to its peers. Border routers then deliver traffic destined for the name server to the nearest instantiation based on routing metrics.

Servers should be placed at locations with topologic diversity—ideally near the organization's peering points with other networks. This ensures clients in different parts of the network topology reach different server instances.
sections.eli5: Each server has two addresses: one shared by all copies for answering queries, and one unique address just for that server's management.

sections.title: Zone Synchronization and Failover
sections.content:
All servers in the mesh must coordinate zone file updates to ensure consistent responses. Zone files should be delivered to the administrative interfaces using secure file transfer methods. Updates should be synchronized across all servers before they become active, using coordinated switch-over times. If a server fails to receive or switch over to new zone data, it should shut down its DNS process rather than serve stale data, allowing DNS failover mechanisms to select other servers.

The RFC recommends using synchronized clocks and a multi-step distribution process: receipt and integrity check at a distribution host, distribution to all mesh servers, integrity verification at each server, coordinated switchover, and a failure process to halt unsynced servers.
sections.eli5: All copies get the same zone information at the same time. If one copy misses an update, it stops answering so people use a different copy.

sections.title: Routing Challenges and Mitigation
sections.content:
One challenge is that routers forwarding traffic to the shared unicast address may have multiple available routes, and those routes may reach different instances of the server. For DNS (which uses independent UDP request-response messages), this is not a problem. For TCP or multi-packet protocols, split-destination failures can occur if a router uses per-packet load sharing or if topology changes shift the cost metrics of available paths.

This is mitigated by the fact that DNS relies heavily on UDP, by careful placement at topologically diverse locations, and by the prevalence of load sharing mechanisms that avoid per-packet distribution. For maximum reliability, at least one authoritative server for each zone should not participate in any shared-unicast mesh. Servers using shared unicast addresses should also avoid ICMP path MTU discovery since ICMP responses might arrive at a different mesh member.
sections.eli5: Sometimes a router might send packets from the same query to different copies of the server. This rarely breaks DNS because DNS queries are small and independent.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The architecture increases some risks and decreases others. The larger number of physical servers increases the risk that misconfiguration or unpatched vulnerabilities will affect one instance, potentially creating a breach. The entity operating the mesh must ensure patches and security mechanisms are applied uniformly. Genetic diversity (using code from different bases) across meshes can help defend against code-based vulnerabilities.

Distribution of zone files is a critical security point. Man-in-the-middle attacks during file transfer could inject false information. Use encrypted transport, digital signatures, and tight access control lists restricted to the administrative interfaces (not the shared unicast address). Conversely, the increased number of servers reduces the impact of denial-of-service attacks and single points of failure from machine crashes or localized disasters.
sections.eli5: More servers mean more chances for mistakes, but also more protection against attacks that take down one server.
